docs.title: How Each Lab Is Built
docs.text:
Every investigation follows the same structure a SOC ticket would:

  1. Alert or objective. What fired, or what I set out to find.
  2. Evidence. Raw logs, packets, or headers, with the queries used to pull them.
  3. Timeline and findings. What happened, in order, backed by artifacts.
  4. Verdict. True positive or false positive, severity, and escalation call.
  5. Detection. A rule that catches it next time, tested against the same data.

Raw evidence and detection rules live in the GitHub repo so every result can be reproduced.

docs.title: Suspicious LSASS Memory Access (Splunk SPL)
docs.text:
index=botsv1 "<EventID>10</EventID>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name="SourceImage">(?<SourceImage>[^<]+)</Data>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name="TargetImage">(?<TargetImage>[^<]+)</Data>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name="GrantedAccess">(?<GrantedAccess>[^<]+)</Data>"
| rex field=_raw "<Computer>(?<host_name>[^<]+)</Computer>"
| where match(TargetImage, "(?i)\\\\lsass\.exe$")
| where match(GrantedAccess, "(?i)^0x(1fffff|1010|1410|1438|143a|1f3fff)$")
| where NOT match(SourceImage, "(?i)^C:\\\\Windows\\\\System32\\\\(svchost|wininit|csrss|services|lsm)\.exe$")
| eval severity=if(match(SourceImage, "(?i)\\\\(AppData|Temp|Users\\\\Public)\\\\"), "critical", "high")
| stats count min(_time) as first_seen max(_time) as last_seen values(GrantedAccess) as access by host_name SourceImage severity
| sort - count
View Sigma Rule Version 
title: Suspicious Process Access to LSASS Memory
status: experimental
author: Mian Talha Nayyar
tags:
  - attack.credential_access

logsource:
  product: windows
  category: process_access
detection:
  selection:
    TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    GrantedAccess:
      - '0x1fffff'
      - '0x1010'
      - '0x1410'
      - '0x1438'
      - '0x143a'
      - '0x1f3fff'
  filter_system:
    SourceImage:
      - 'C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe'
      - 'C:\Windows\System32\wininit.exe'
      - 'C:\Windows\System32\csrss.exe'
      - 'C:\Windows\System32\services.exe'
      - 'C:\Windows\System32\lsm.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_system
falsepositives:
  - EDR and antivirus agents (add their paths after baselining)
  - Administrators creating a dump from Task Manager
level: high

docs.title: Lab 01: Windows Telemetry & Process Creation Auditing (Event ID 4688)
docs.text:
• Date: October 2026
  • Category: Endpoint Telemetry & Incident Analysis
  • Framework Mapping: MITRE ATT&CK [T1059 - Command and Scripting Interpreter] / [T1082 - System Information Discovery]
  • Target OS: Windows 10/11 Enterprise

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary & Objective
docs.text:
Adversaries routinely execute native binaries (Living off the Land) to enumerate accounts, query network configurations, and spawn malicious payloads. By default, Windows does not log granular process execution data.

The objective of this lab was to configure Audit Process Creation within the Local Security Policy, generate process execution telemetry, and analyze the resulting Event ID 4688 forensic artifacts to understand parent-child process relationships.

docs.title: 2. Methodology & Configuration
docs.text:
1. Auditing Policy Configuration:
  2. Navigated to Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > System Audit Policies > Detailed Tracking.
  3. Enabled Audit Process Creation for both Success and Failure.
  4. Log Acquisition:
  5. Monitored the Security event log via Windows Event Viewer (eventvwr.msc).
  6. Filtered telemetry using event filter EventID == 4688.

docs.title: Telemetry Overview: Filtered Security Event Stream
Key Artifact Breakdown:
docs.text:
• Event ID: 4688 (A new process has been created)
  • Account / Security ID: SYSTEM (Authority/System-level context)
  • New Process Name: C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe (The spawned binary)
  • Creator (Parent) Process Name: C:\Windows\System32\services.exe (The launching binary)
  • Mandatory Label: System Mandatory Level (High integrity execution token)

docs.title: Analytical Insight:
docs.text: In a typical enterprise SOC environment, mapping the Parent Process (Creator Process Name) to the Child Process (New Process Name) establishes the process lineage. While services.exe spawning svchost.exe represents expected baseline activity, an anomalous parent (such as winword.exe spawning cmd.exe or powershell.exe) would represent a high-confidence indicator of compromise (IOC) indicative of macro exploitation.

docs.title: 4. Defensive Takeaways for SOC Triage
docs.text:
• Baseline Profiling: Knowing what should launch a process is just as important as knowing what the binary does. Legitimate system binaries executing under abnormal parents must be flagged immediately.
  • Log Enrichment: Standard 4688 logging provides binary names, but enabling the sub-setting "Include command line in process creation events" adds the full CLI arguments, essential for identifying obfuscated scripts (e.g., base64-encoded PowerShell).

docs.title: Lab 02: Network Traffic Analysis & Cleartext HTTP Stream Reconstruction
docs.text:
• Date: October 2026
  • Category: Network Security & Packet Forensics
  • Framework Mapping: MITRE ATT&CK [T1071.001 - Web Protocols] / [TA0011 - Command and Control]
  • Tooling: Wireshark, Protocol Hierarchy, TCP Stream Analysis

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary & Objective
docs.text:
Network telemetry provides an objective source of truth during defensive triage, exposing external communications even if endpoint logs are absent or purged.

The objective of this lab was to triage a packet capture (.cap), identify active layer-3 and layer-4 conversations across modern IPv6 infrastructure, isolate unencrypted application-layer requests, and reconstruct the full bidirectional TCP session to extract key forensic indicators.

docs.title: 2. Triage Methodology
docs.text:
1. Endpoint & Protocol Enumeration:
  2. Evaluated the global protocol distribution using Wireshark Protocol Hierarchy.
  3. Identified active communication channels via the IPv6 Endpoints table.
  4. Display Filter Application:
  5. Applied the display filter http.request to isolate client-initiated web requests from transport-layer overhead.
  6. Layer 7 Stream Reconstruction:
  7. Reconstructed the complete conversational flow using Follow TCP Stream to inspect request headers and server responses.

docs.title: Telemetry Overview: HTTP Request Frame Isolation
Key Artifact Breakdown:
docs.text:
• Frame ID: 49
  • Protocol: HTTP/1.0
  • Source IP (Client): 2001:6f8:102d:0:2d0:9ff:fee3:e8de
  • Destination IP (Host): 2001:6f8:900:7c0::2
  • Destination Port: 80 (Standard HTTP)
  • Source Port: 59201 (Ephemeral Client Port)
  • Host Header: cl-1985.ham-01.de.sixxs.net
  • User-Agent: Lynx/2.8.6rel.2 libwww-FM/2.14 SSL-MM/1.4.1 OpenSSL/0.9.8b
  • Response Code: HTTP/1.1 200 OK (Apache Web Server)

docs.title: Analytical Insight:
docs.text:
• Cleartext Visibility: Because the transaction occurred over unencrypted HTTP (port 80), all request headers, user agents, and response payloads are exposed.
  • Client Fingerprinting: The User-Agent string identifies a terminal-based web browser (Lynx), rather than a standard GUI browser like Chrome or Edge. In an enterprise environment, non-standard user agents originating from end-user workstations warrant immediate investigation as potential script execution or automated tooling.
  • Content Inspection: The server returned an open directory listing exposing downloadable files (.pdf, .htm). In a real incident scenario, any retrieved binaries would be carved via File > Export Objects > HTTP and submitted for hash analysis.

docs.title: 4. Defensive Takeaways for SOC Triage
docs.text:
• Network Baselines: Modern enterprise web communications are overwhelmingly encrypted via TLS (port 443). Outbound cleartext HTTP (port 80) should be monitored and flagged for inspection.
  • Full-Session Context: Individual packet inspection shows fragmented data; following the TCP stream reconstructs the entire conversational context needed for defensible incident reporting.

docs.title: Lab 03: SIEM Threat Hunting & LSASS Credential Dumping Detection
docs.text:
• Date: October 2026
  • Category: SIEM Detection Engineering & Threat Hunting
  • Framework Mapping: MITRE ATT&CK [T1003.001 - OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory] / [TA0006 - Credential Access]
  • Tooling: Splunk Enterprise, Search Processing Language (SPL), Sysmon (Event ID 10)

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary & Objective
docs.text:
Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (lsass.exe) enforces security policy and stores active authentication credentials, Kerberos tickets, and NTLM hashes in process memory. Adversaries routinely target LSASS to harvest credentials for domain-wide lateral movement.

The objective of this investigation was to ingest high-fidelity endpoint security telemetry into Splunk, build regular expression field extractions against raw Sysmon XML, and engineer a robust detection query (SPL) that exposes unauthorized attempts to access and dump LSASS memory.

docs.title: 2. Telemetry & Attack Surface
docs.text:
• Data Source: Sysmon Operational Logs (Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon)
  • Event ID: 10 (ProcessAccess)
  • Target Process: C:\Windows\System32\lsass.exe
  • Simulated Adversary: Atomic Red Team (T1003.001)

docs.title: Phase 1: Ingestion & Telemetry Exploration
docs.text:
An initial hunt query across the dedicated botsv1 index isolated all events referencing the LSASS credential vault: 

index=botsv1 "lsass.exe"
![Credential Dumping Artifacts Table](../assets/images/lab03-splunk-hunt.png)
The search isolated 851 raw sysmon records detailing process access attempts against the local authority service

---
### Phase 2: SPL Field Extraction & Aggregation
Because the raw log payload contained nested XML attributes without native schema parsing, a targeted regular expression (rex) query was constructed to extract the requesting binary (SourceImage) and aggregate execution frequency:
```spl
index=botsv1 "lsass.exe" "<EventID>10</EventID>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name="SourceImage">(?<SourceImage>[^<]+)</Data>"
| stats count by SourceImage

![Credential Dumping Artifacts Table](../assets/images/lab03-splunk-table.png)
---
## 4. Forensic Findings & Malicious Artifacts Identified

The analytical query exposed multiple adversary tools accessing LSASS:

| Requesting Image (`SourceImage`) | Invocations | Threat Classification |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `Outflank-Dumpert.exe` | 2 | Custom Red-Team LSASS Memory Dumper |
| `procdump.exe` / `procdump64.exe` | 6 | Weaponized Sysinternals Dump Utility |
| `notprocdump.exe` | 1 | Defense Evasion (Renamed Binary) |
| `AppData\Local\Temp\*.exe` | 38 | Dropped Binary from Temp Directory |
| `powershell.exe` | 1 | Scripted Credential Ingestion (`Invoke-Mimikatz`) |
| `rundll32.exe` | 2 | LOLBin (`comsvcs.dll` MiniDump execution) |

---

## 5. SOC Detection Engineering Takeaways
1. **Filename-Agnostic Rules:** Attackers frequently disguise binaries (evidenced by `notprocdump.exe`). Detections should alert on the **TargetImage** (`lsass.exe`) combined with abnormal **GrantedAccess** permissions (e.g., `0x1010`, `0x1F0FFF`), rather than relying solely on the process filename.
2. **Untrusted Path Baselines:** Any process originating from `AppData\Local\Temp` or non-standard paths that accesses `lsass.exe` represents high-confidence malicious behavior and should generate immediate Priority-1 alerts in the SOC.

### Production Detection Rule (Splunk Enterprise / Cloud)

```spl
index=botsv1 sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventCode=10
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name TargetImage"">(?<TargetImage>[^<]+)</Data>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name SourceImage"">(?<SourceImage>[^<]+)</Data>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data GrantedAccess"" Name>(?<GrantedAccess>[^<]+)</Data>"
| search TargetImage="*\\lsass.exe" GrantedAccess IN ("0x1010", "0x1410", "0x1F0FFF", "0x1438", "0x143a")
| search NOT SourceImage IN (
    "*\\Program Files\\Windows Defender\\*", 
    "*\\Program Files\\Microsoft Security Client\\*",
    "*\\System32\\svchost.exe", 
    "*\\System32\\csrss.exe", 
    "*\\System32\\services.exe"
  )
| stats count earliest(_time) as first_seen latest(_time) as last_seen by SourceImage, TargetImage, GrantedAccess
| convert ctime(first_seen) ctime(last_seen)

Rule Logic & Triage Notes: - Target Filter: Isolates calls requesting handles to lsass.exe. - Access Rights Filter: Filters on dangerous masks (0x1010 = PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION + PROCESS_VM_READ, and 0x1F0FFF = PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS). - Baseline Exclusions: Suppresses routine antivirus and core operating system processes to minimize false positives.

docs.title: Lab 04: Inbound Phishing Analysis & Header Forensics
docs.text:
• Date: October 2026
  • Category: Phishing Triage & Threat Vector Analysis
  • Framework Mapping: MITRE ATT&CK [T1566.001 - Spearphishing Attachment] / [T1566.002 - Spearphishing Link] / [TA0001 - Initial Access]
  • Tooling: RFC 822 Header Parsers, URL Defanging, CyberChef, Static Document Analysis

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary & Objective
docs.text:
Phishing remains the primary initial access vector exploited by threat actors to harvest enterprise credentials, establish command-and-control footholds, and drop secondary payloads. Modern phishing campaigns leverage brand impersonation, visual typosquatting, and multi-stage delivery chains to bypass automated boundary email gateways.

The objective of this investigation was to triage suspicious inbound emails, dissect RFC 822 header metadata for sender-address discrepancies, trace multi-hop URL redirections, analyze tracking web beacons, and evaluate weaponized document attachments across multiple real-world phishing scenarios.

docs.title: 2. Attack Vectors & Telemetry Analyzed
docs.text:
• Target Mailbox Environment: Standard Enterprise Gateway / Yahoo / Outlook
  • Key Protocols: SMTP, RFC 822, MIME
  • Primary Attack Surfaces:
  • Display Name Spoofing & Visual Impersonation (Netllx billing)
  • Tracking Pixels & Read Receipt Telemetry (tracking.png)
  • URL Shorteners & Multi-Stage Redirection Portals
  • Malicious Attachments (.pdf, .dot, .xlsx)

docs.title: Phase 1: Header Analysis & Sender Authentication Discrepancies
docs.text:
Triage of suspicious transaction receipts and account suspension warnings revealed deliberate discrepancies between the asserted display names and the authentic originating addresses:

  • Impersonated Brand: service@paypal.com routed from envelope sender sultanbogor.com.
  • Typo-Squatted Impersonation: A simulated Netflix suspension notice used the display name Netllx billing (substituting the letters "fi" with "ll") while routing from the unauthenticated external domain z99@musacombi.online.

Attackers exploit the default UI behavior of modern mail clients, which prominently display user-configurable display names while concealing the underlying routing path.

docs.title: Phase 2: Link Obfuscation, Tracking Pixels & Redirection Chains
docs.text:
Inspection of raw HTML bodies exposed multiple obfuscation techniques engineered to evade automated boundary scanning:

  1. Shortened Redirection URLs: Phishing lures utilized URL shorteners (https://is.gd/6oCJ4m) to mask destination landing pages during transit.
  2. Web Beacon Telemetry: An embedded 1x1 image (tracking.png hosted on devret[.]xyz) served as an active tracking pixel, silently notifying the adversary that the target mailbox was active.
  3. Multi-Stage Redirection Portals: Clickable lures routed targets through simulated cloud-sharing hops (Citrix $\rightarrow$ OneDrive $\rightarrow$ Adobe) before terminating at an external credential harvesting interface mimicking an enterprise Microsoft Outlook portal.

docs.title: Phase 3: Weaponized Attachments & Payload Analysis
docs.text:
When direct external links are blocked by strict email gateway filters, adversaries pivot to weaponized attachments:

  • Remote Template Ingestion (.dot): A fake Apple billing notification arrived with a blank email body, delivering a .dot Microsoft Word Template configured to pull remote malicious macros upon opening.
  • Macro Execution via Spreadsheet (.xlsx): A fake DHL courier notice delivered a spreadsheet instructing the victim to enable content, initiating execution of the native Windows binary regasm.exe.

docs.title: 4. Forensic Findings & Extracted IOCs
docs.text: Artifact Type Raw Indicator Defanged / Normalized IOC Context / Threat Intent Sender Domain sultanbogor.com sultanbogor[.]com Unauthorized SMTP relay for PayPal brand spoofing Sender Address z99@musacombi.online z99@musacombi[.]online Impersonation of Netflix billing operations Tracking Domain http://devret.xyz hxxp://devret[.]xyz Tracking pixel delivery & mailbox enumeration Shortened Link https://is.gd/6oCJ4m hxxps://is[.]gd/6oCJ4m URL obfuscation hiding credential landing page Attachment Apple_Receipt.dot Apple_Receipt.dot Template injection / macro download vector Child Executable regasm.exe regasm.exe Living-off-the-land utility targeted for execution

docs.title: 5. SOC Analyst Detection & Response Engineering
docs.text:
1. Enforce Strict Domain Alignment (DMARC/SPF/DKIM): Configure mail gateway policies to reject or quarantine inbound messages where the RFC 5322 From domain fails SPF alignment or lacks valid DKIM cryptographical signing from the asserted organization.
  2. Block Inbound External Templates & Dangerous Extensions: Restrict inbound mail containing macro-enabled templates (.dot, .dotm, .xltm) at the secure email gateway (SEG), as legitimate external business correspondence rarely requires foreign template definitions.
  3. Automated URL Defanging & Sandbox Detonation: Ensure security orchestration platforms (SOAR) automatically parse reported .eml files, defang all embedded links, expand shorteners in isolated sandboxes, and query domains against live threat intelligence feeds.
